analogy.p: Imagine the computer is a library. The operating system is the librarian who runs the building. Utility software is the specialist crew: a locksmith who puts valuable books in locked cases that need a key to open (encryption); a shelving team who bring the scattered volumes of a series back together on one shelf so they are quick to fetch (defragmentation); and a packing team who squash books into smaller boxes for storage or posting (compression). The analogy breaks down because a real book is not fragmented across the library and, with lossy compression, real books cannot lose pages permanently and still be the same book.
analogy.t: A caretaker and tidy-up crew for a library

bullets: Utility software is **system software**: it maintains and supports the computer instead of producing a document or game for the user.
The specification names three utilities: **encryption software**, **defragmentation** and **data compression**. Learn what each does, how it does it and why it is useful.
Other utilities exist in real life (for example anti-malware, backup and disk clean-up tools) and you can use them as extra examples, but the three named ones are the ones to know in detail.
Utilities may be built into the OS or installed separately.
Many run only when the user starts them (for example a defrag scan or compressing a folder); some run continuously (anti-malware scans).
Link to 1.5.1: the OS manages the computer while utilities improve how well it runs; link to 1.4.2: encryption is a method of preventing data theft; link to 1.2: compression saves storage space.
core.h: What utility software is and where it fits
core.p: **Utility software** is a type of **system software** designed to help **analyse, configure, optimise or maintain** a computer. It is separate from the operating system, although many operating systems include basic utilities. It is different from **application software**, which lets the user do a task such as writing or gaming. OCR J277 1.5.2 asks you to know the purpose and functionality of utility software and, specifically, to be able to describe three types: **encryption software, defragmentation and data compression**. Utilities generally work in the background or on request to keep the system secure, efficient and tidy.

bullets: **Plaintext** = the original readable data. **Ciphertext** = the scrambled data. **Key** = the secret value used by the algorithm to encrypt or decrypt.
Encryption does **not** stop someone stealing or copying a file; it stops them **understanding** it.
Software can encrypt a **single file**, a **folder**, a **whole hard drive** or a USB stick, so a lost laptop does not mean lost data.
Encryption is also used when data travels on a network (such as online banking, shown by https and a padlock), so that anyone who intercepts the data sees only ciphertext.
Without the key, decrypting is extremely hard because there are billions of possible keys, so brute force takes far too long.
If the user **forgets the key or password**, the data may be lost permanently.
Encryption uses processing power and takes time, so large amounts of data may slow the computer slightly.
Link to 1.4.2: encryption is listed as a method for preventing vulnerabilities, because it protects against interception of data.
core.h: Encryption software: what it is and how it works
core.p: **Encryption** is the process of scrambling data using an **algorithm** and a **key** so that it cannot be understood by anyone who does not have the key. Data before encryption is called **plaintext** and the scrambled result is called **ciphertext**. Encryption software performs this process automatically on files, folders, whole drives or messages. To read the data again it must be **decrypted** using the correct key, which turns the ciphertext back into plaintext. The purpose is to keep data **confidential**: if it is stolen, intercepted or lost, it is useless to the attacker.

bullets: **Stored data** (at rest): files on laptops, phones, USB sticks and servers can be encrypted to protect them if the device is stolen.
**Data in transit**: websites using https encrypt the connection so passwords and card details cannot be read by an eavesdropper.
**Messaging apps** often use end-to-end encryption so only the sender and receiver can read messages.
Organisations that hold personal data have a legal duty to protect it: encryption helps meet the requirements of the Data Protection Act 2018.
Encryption protects against **interception** and **theft**, but not against a user giving away their password (social engineering).
An encrypted drive is useless to a thief, which reduces the harm of a data breach even when the physical device is lost.
Weighing it up: benefits are confidentiality and legal compliance; drawbacks are processing time, the risk of losing the key and the need for staff training.
core.h: Why and when encryption is used
core.p: Encryption is chosen when data is sensitive and the damage of it falling into the wrong hands would be serious. Examples include customers' personal and financial details, medical records, private messages and company secrets. Laws such as the **Data Protection Act 2018** require organisations to keep personal data secure, and encryption is a common way to demonstrate this. It is especially important for portable devices, which are easily lost or stolen, and for data sent across networks, where it can be intercepted.

bullets: A **fragmented** file is one whose blocks are stored in **non-contiguous** (not next to each other) locations.
Fragmentation happens because files are repeatedly **created, edited and deleted**, leaving small gaps of free space across the disk.
On an HDD, the read/write head and spinning platter must **move to find each fragment**, so reading a fragmented file takes longer than a file stored in one place.
Fragmentation therefore causes slower file access, slower start-up of programs and a slower computer overall.
The problem builds up gradually as the disk fills and files are changed more often.
It does not usually affect data **correctness**: all the data is still there, just stored in scattered pieces.
The solution is a utility called a **defragmenter**.
core.p: When files are saved on a **magnetic hard disk drive (HDD)**, the OS stores them in small blocks. At first the blocks of a file are stored next to each other. As files are edited, grown, deleted and new ones saved, the free space becomes broken up into small gaps. The OS then stores new or larger files in whatever gaps are available, so the pieces of one file end up in different places. This is called **fragmentation**. The read/write head of an HDD must move physically to each piece, which takes time, so the computer becomes slower to open and save files.

bullets: The utility analyses the disk, moves file fragments so that each file is stored in **one continuous section**, and groups the free space together.
Because the pieces are now next to each other, the read/write head makes **fewer movements**, which **reduces access time** and speeds up reading and writing.
Joined free space means new files can also be stored contiguously, which **slows the return** of fragmentation.

Defragmenting is **not** needed (and not recommended) for **solid state drives (SSDs)** because they have no moving parts, so scattered data is not slower to read; extra rewrites would also wear flash memory.
Defragmentation does **not** free up space or delete files; the amount of free space stays the same.
It can take a long time on a large, heavily fragmented disk, and the computer may run slowly while it is working.
Many operating systems run defragmentation automatically on a schedule.
Exam link: 'explain why defragmentation makes a computer faster' needs: pieces together, less head movement, faster access.
core.p: **Defragmentation** (or **defragmenter**) software reorganises the data on a hard disk so that the blocks belonging to each file are stored **together (contiguously)**, and so that the free space is gathered into one large block. It does this by reading scattered pieces and rewriting them next to each other. The result is that the read/write head has to move much less to read a file, so files open faster and the computer is more responsive. It also makes new files more likely to be stored in one piece.

bullets: **Purpose of compression**: save storage space, reduce transmission time and reduce bandwidth used.
Examples: zipping a folder before emailing it, streaming music and video, images on websites, game downloads.
A compressed file normally has to be **decompressed** (extracted) before it is opened; the exception is formats such as MP3 and JPEG that devices decode on the fly.
The **compression ratio** or the **percentage saving** describes how effective the compression is.
Compression works by finding **patterns and repetition** or by removing data the user will not notice is missing.
There are two types: **lossy** and **lossless** (see the next two sections); you must be able to describe both and choose between them.
Compression needs processing time to compress and decompress, so there is a trade-off between smaller files and CPU effort.
core.p: **Data compression** reduces the size of a file so that it takes up less storage space and can be transmitted faster. **Compression software** uses an algorithm to find a smaller way to represent the same data. A compressed file is smaller in bytes, which means that more files fit on a drive or attachment limit, and downloads or uploads take less time and use less bandwidth. Before the file can be used it must usually be **decompressed**, which converts it back to a usable form.

bullets: **Lossless**: no data lost, original perfectly recovered. Examples: ZIP, PNG, FLAC. Used for text, program files, spreadsheets and where accuracy matters.
**Lossy**: some data permanently removed, original cannot be restored. Examples: JPEG images, MP3 audio, MP4 video. Used for photos, music and video where small quality loss is acceptable.
Lossy gives **smaller files** than lossless, but **quality is reduced**; the more you compress, the worse the quality.
Lossless is essential for text and software: if even one character is lost the file could become unreadable or the program could crash.
Lossy compression is **irreversible**: saving a JPEG repeatedly reduces quality each time, so keep an uncompressed original.
Choosing between them depends on the purpose: **streaming a film over a slow connection** (lossy), **archiving legal documents** (lossless).
Run-length encoding example: AAAABBB becomes 4A3B, which is lossless as the original can be rebuilt exactly (7 characters stored as 4).
core.p: The two types of compression are different in what they do with data. **Lossless compression** reduces file size without losing any information: when the file is decompressed it is **identical to the original**. It works by encoding repeated data more efficiently, for example by replacing repeated sequences with shorter codes (as in run-length encoding or dictionary methods). **Lossy compression** reduces file size by **permanently removing** some data that is considered less important, such as sounds humans cannot hear or fine detail in an image the eye is unlikely to notice. The original cannot be restored exactly, but the file can be much smaller.

bullets: Saving = original size − compressed size.
Percentage saving = (saving ÷ original size) × 100. Example: 20 MB → 5 MB saves 15 MB, which is (15 ÷ 20) × 100 = **75%**.
Compression ratio = original ÷ compressed. Example: 20 ÷ 5 = 4, a ratio of 4:1.
Download time = size in megabits ÷ speed in megabits per second. Convert megabytes to megabits by multiplying by 8.
Example: 30 MB at 8 Mbps: 30 × 8 = 240 Mb, 240 ÷ 8 = 30 seconds. After compression to 12 MB: 12 × 8 = 96 Mb, 96 ÷ 8 = 12 seconds.
Always include **units** (MB, seconds, %) in your final answer.
Check your answer is sensible: the compressed file must be smaller than the original, and the percentage must be between 0 and 100.
core.p: Exam questions sometimes give file sizes before and after compression and ask for the saving or for the effect on download time. The **saving** is the original size minus the compressed size. The **percentage saving** is the saving divided by the original size, multiplied by 100. For transmission time use **time = file size (in bits) ÷ transfer rate (in bits per second)**, remembering that 1 byte = 8 bits and that file sizes are often in megabytes while connection speeds are in megabits per second.

bullets: **Encryption**: problem = data could be read if stolen/intercepted; action = scrambles data using a key; benefit = confidentiality; limitation = need the key, takes processing time.

**Defragmentation**: problem = files split into scattered fragments on an HDD; action = rearranges so each file is stored together; benefit = faster access; limitation = no use for SSDs, can take time.
**Compression**: problem = files too big to store or send quickly; action = reduces file size; benefit = saves space and time; limitation = lossy loses quality, needs decompressing.

In a scenario about **emailing a large file**, recommend compression; about **a lost laptop containing customer data**, recommend encryption; about **a slow old hard-drive computer**, recommend defragmentation.
Only one of the three is about security (encryption); do not give defragmentation or compression as ways to protect data.
Remember that utilities are **not the OS**: the OS has its own functions of memory, file, user and peripheral management.
Higher-level extension: combining them is common, for example compressing a folder and then encrypting it before sending.
core.p: It helps to compare the three utilities by asking four questions: what problem does it solve, what does it do, what is the benefit and what is the limitation. Encryption solves a **security** problem, defragmentation solves a **performance** problem on hard drives, and compression solves a **storage and transfer** problem. Each is a form of system software that the user can run to look after the computer or its data, and each can be justified in a scenario if you link it to what the scenario needs.

bullets: Typical marks: 'State what is meant by utility software' [1-2]; 'Describe how defragmentation works' [2-3]; 'Explain why compression is useful' [2-3]; 'Discuss' type questions [6].
Always name the utility, **say what it does** and then give the **benefit**.
A good definition: 'Utility software is system software that helps to maintain and optimise the computer.'
Distinguish clearly between **utility software** (maintains the computer) and the **operating system** (manages the hardware and runs programs).
Link to **1.2.2**: HDD and SSD behave differently; mention this when discussing defragmentation.
Link to **1.3**: compression reduces the bandwidth and time needed to send data over a network.
Link to **1.4**: encryption helps protect against interception and keeps personal data secure under the law.
Practise by writing a one-sentence description of each utility from memory.
core.h: Link to the wider course and how it is examined
core.p: Utility software is examined in short questions on Paper 1: Computer systems. You may be asked to state, describe or explain, or to match utilities to scenarios. It combines well with security (1.4), data storage (1.2) and the operating system (1.5.1), so it can appear inside a longer discussion question. The key to marks is accurate description of what the utility does followed by a consequence in the context given.

exam: **State** questions (1-2 marks): 'State two utility programs' needs two of encryption, defragmentation, compression.
**Define utility software**: 'system software that helps to maintain and optimise a computer' earns the mark; 'software for the user' does not.
**Describe defragmentation** [2-3]: rearranges file fragments so each file is stored together; free space is grouped; less head movement.
**Explain why defragmentation speeds up a computer**: pieces in one place, read/write head moves less, so quicker access to data.
**Describe encryption** [2-3]: data is scrambled using an algorithm and a key; unreadable without the key; turns plaintext into ciphertext.
Always mention that encryption makes data **meaningless/unreadable**, not that it blocks access; the latter is a common lost mark.
**Lossy v lossless** [4]: lossy permanently removes data, smaller file, quality lost; lossless keeps all data, file bigger, original restored.
For **choose and justify** questions, name the type, link to the scenario (e.g. 'streaming video, so lossy because quality loss is small') and give the benefit.
For calculation questions show working: percentage saving = saving ÷ original × 100, and give units.
In a 6-mark question cover at least three utilities, describe each, give a benefit and a limitation and finish with a conclusion.
Link to the scenario: 'laptop stolen' = encryption, 'old slow HDD' = defragmentation, 'emailing a large file' = compression.

mistakes.r: Defragmentation rearranges existing data so files are stored together; it does not delete anything or increase free space.
Defragmentation is for magnetic hard disk drives; SSDs have no moving parts, so it gives no benefit.
Encryption does not stop access to the data; it makes the stolen data unreadable without the key.
mistakes.w: Encryption stops hackers getting the data.

mistakes.r: Lossless keeps the original; lossy permanently removes some data and reduces quality.
mistakes.w: Compression always keeps the original quality.

mistakes.r: Lossy is irreversible: the removed data cannot be recovered.
Utility software is system software that maintains the computer, separate from the OS, which manages hardware and runs programs.
mistakes.w: Utility software is the same as the operating system.

mistakes.r: A password controls access; encryption scrambles the data itself using a key.
mistakes.w: Encryption is the same as a password.

mistakes.r: Compression makes files smaller, so they use less storage and are quicker to send; they usually must be decompressed to be used.
mistakes.w: Compression makes a file faster to open.

mistakes.r: Fragmentation only means the pieces are stored in different places; the data is complete.
mistakes.w: A fragmented file has been corrupted.

summary: OCR J277 1.5.2 asks you to know the purpose and functionality of utility software, and to describe encryption software, defragmentation and data compression. It matters because Paper 1 questions ask you to state what each does, explain why it helps and choose the right utility for a scenario.

terms.d: System software that helps to analyse, configure, optimise or maintain a computer.
Software that runs and maintains the computer, including the operating system and utility software.
Scrambling data using an algorithm and a key so that it cannot be understood without the key.
Data in its original readable form before encryption.
Data that has been encrypted and cannot be read without decryption.
A secret value used by the encryption algorithm to encrypt and decrypt data.
Converting ciphertext back into plaintext using the correct key.
When the blocks of a file are stored in different, non-contiguous places on a disk.
A utility that rearranges the blocks on a hard disk so that each file is stored in one continuous section and free space is grouped together.
Stored next to each other with no gaps.
The part of a hard disk drive that moves over the platter to read and write data.
Reducing the size of a file so it takes up less storage space and is faster to transmit.
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data; the original can be restored exactly.
Compression that permanently removes some data to make the file smaller; the original cannot be restored.
Restoring a compressed file to a usable form.
The amount of data that can be transmitted in a given time.
Secondary storage with no moving parts that stores data in flash memory.

worked.q: A 24 MB file is compressed to 6 MB. Calculate the percentage saving. [2 marks]

worked.ans: Compression saves 18 seconds (30 s down to 12 s).
worked.q: A video file of 30 MB is downloaded at 8 megabits per second. It can be compressed to 12 MB. Calculate how many seconds compression saves. [4 marks]

worked.ans: Over time the blocks of a file become scattered across the hard disk. Defragmentation rearranges them so each file is stored in one continuous section. The read/write head then has to move less to find the data, so files open and save faster. [3 marks]
worked.q: Explain how defragmentation can make a computer with a hard disk drive run faster. [3 marks]
steps: State the problem: files are stored in fragments in different places.
State the action: defragmentation moves the pieces so each file is stored together.
State the consequence: the read/write head moves less, so data is accessed faster.
